analysis.one_liner: Bars federal agencies from counting the dollar cost of climate damage in their rules.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the House Natural Resources Committee 18–15 but never received a House floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would prohibit the Department of Energy, the EPA, the Department of the Interior, and the Council on Environmental Quality from using the 'social cost of carbon, methane, or nitrous oxide' — the dollar estimate of the damage one more ton of emissions does — in any rulemaking, guidance, or agency action [S2][S3]. Agencies could only use such estimates again if Congress passed a law explicitly authorizing it, or if the estimate followed the stricter OMB Circular A-4 rules: 3 and 7 percent discount rates and counting only costs and benefits inside the United States [S2][S3]. The bill also directs the EPA to report how many rules since January 2009 used these cost estimates [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Fossil fuel producers, especially coal companies and oil and gas drillers. The social cost of carbon is the number agencies plug into cost-benefit analyses to show that limits on pollution outweigh industry compliance costs; removing it makes climate and methane rules much harder to justify and easier to overturn in court. The bill text itself singles out the social cost of methane that the EPA used in its 2015–2016 oil and gas methane rules and the Interior Department used in its 2016 rule limiting methane waste on federal lands [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits four agencies from considering the social cost of carbon, methane, or nitrous oxide in any cost-benefit analysis, rulemaking, guidance, or other action, unless Congress enacts a law authorizing it [S2][S3].

Allows a social-cost estimate only if it complies with OMB Circular A-4, uses 3 and 7 percent discount rates, and counts only domestic costs and benefits — conditions that shrink the measured damage from emissions dramatically, since climate change is global and damages compound over long horizons [S2][S3].
Requires the EPA to report the number of rulemakings, guidance documents, and agency actions since January 2009 that used these social-cost estimates [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people, through the climate damages and air pollution that would no longer be counted when agencies weigh pollution limits. Rules justified in part by the social cost of carbon — including limits on methane leaks from oil and gas operations and greenhouse gas standards — would become harder to defend, and the cost of those damages would fall on the public rather than appear on any ledger [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone exposed to pollution and climate damage

drawbacks.text: The bill's methodological critique has some basis: the interagency working group's estimates used discount rates other than the 3 and 7 percent in OMB Circular A-4 and counted global rather than domestic benefits, which supporters argue departs from the government's own cost-benefit standards [S3].

However, the ban goes far beyond fixing methodology: it forbids considering these costs in 'any action' by four agencies, and restricting the accounting to domestic effects while using high discount rates would leave most climate damage — which falls on future generations and on people outside U.S. borders — out of the government's math entirely [S3].
Agencies would lose a widely used tool for quantifying the harm of emissions, making it harder to justify rules that limit methane from oil and gas operations or greenhouse gases generally [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The strongest case for the bill is procedural: the social-cost estimates were developed by an interagency working group without the discount-rate and geographic-scope conventions OMB prescribes, and the bill would force any future estimate through a stricter, congressionally sanctioned framework. But the practical effect is much blunter — it removes the dollar measure of climate damage from four agencies' decisions entirely unless a future estimate clears deliberately narrow conditions, which would make it far harder for the government to justify any limit on carbon or methane pollution. For the fossil fuel producers who benefit, that is the point; for the public, the cost of emissions stops being counted at all.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House Natural Resources Committee but never came up for a vote in the full House before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 29, 2017 and referred to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Natural Resources Committee [S1][S5].
It never advanced in the Energy and Commerce Committee beyond a subcommittee referral; it was reported only by Natural Resources [S5].
The Natural Resources Committee held markups on November 29–30, 2017 and ordered the bill reported (amended) by a vote of 18 to 15 [S5].
The committee reported the bill on November 2, 2018 (H. Rept. 115-999, Part I), but the House never voted on it before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people who benefit from air-quality and climate rules kept the government's tool for counting pollution damage, since the ban never became law. Fossil fuel producers gained nothing from the bill itself, though an existing executive order had already directed agencies toward domestic-only, higher-discount-rate accounting [S3].

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 48 cosponsors were Republicans [S1][S4], and the committee's 18–15 vote fell along the committee's partisan split, though the record does not list each side's party.

industries.note: The bill strips the dollar measure agencies use to justify limits on coal production and use, and its findings single out regulation of coal as a target [S3]. Cheaper-to-produce coal comes at the cost of air pollution and climate damage the government would no longer count.

The bill's definitions and findings specifically target the social cost of methane used in EPA's 2015–2016 oil and gas methane rules and Interior's 2016 rule limiting methane waste on federal lands [S3]. Weak methane limits mean more leaked gas and lower compliance costs for drillers.

industries.industry: Government climate regulation itself (EPA, Interior, DOE, CEQ rulemaking)
industries.note: Four agencies would lose the ability to monetize climate damages in any rulemaking without new congressional authorization, weakening their ability to defend pollution limits in cost-benefit terms [S2][S3].
